strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely gap: finite-sample theoretical analysis of iterative self-improvement, in contrast to prior asymptotic/population-level treatments (Huang et al., Sun et al.). The finite-sample lens (Theorem 4.1) meaningfully explains why infinite-sample idealized updates are inconsistent with observed practice (e.g., saturation, initialization-dependence), which is a genuine conceptual contribution.

The theoretical development is extensive and internally rigorous as far as it can be checked: proofs are given in detail (via Hellinger-distance MLE bounds, fixed-point/interval analyses for iterated maps, and careful Puiseux-series asymptotics for phase-transition behavior). The mathematical machinery (Definition A.1 interval analysis, Corollary B.3 monotonicity in a and ν, Lemma C.1-C.9 for asymptotics) is substantial and mostly self-consistent.

The paper derives concrete, interpretable, and falsifiable qualitative predictions: moderate task difficulty is needed for sustained self-improvement (Remark 4.6.1), larger budgets help and there is an inherent performance ceiling (Remarks 4.6.2-4.6.3), and for easy-to-hard curricula there exist feasibility/improvement conditions governed by difficulty ratio (β′, β), budget (ν), and initialization, with a phase transition in sample budget (Remarks 5.7.1-5.7.4).

Empirical validation is provided both via Monte Carlo simulations of the derived bounds/intervals (Figures 1-2) and via real (if synthetic/small-scale) LLM experiments on a graph shortest-path task with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, showing qualitative agreement with several theoretical predictions (moderate-difficulty regime, budget effects m and n, non-monotonic gap in β′, phase transition in n).

The notation, assumptions, and deferred definitions are systematically organized (Appendix Table 1, Definitions A.1-A.2), which aids reproducibility of the theoretical claims, and hyperparameters/dataset construction for experiments are documented in the appendix (Section D).
weaknesses: The theory rests on strong, somewhat opaque high-level assumptions whose practical validity is not established. Assumption 4.3 (coupling acceptance rate to expected reward via constant c and small γ) and Assumption 5.1 (power-law separation of task difficulties across a neighborhood Θ of pretrained initialization, with constants β, β′ uniform over θ ∈ Θ) are central to essentially every downstream result, yet no empirical evidence is given that these hold (even approximately) for real LLMs/tasks; the shortest-path experiments do not verify the assumptions themselves, only qualitative downstream trends.

The finite model class Π assumption (Theorem 4.1, Remark 4.2) is a strong simplification for a continuous, high-dimensional generative model; the justification given (citing intrinsic-dimension and tree-search-based agent-archive arguments) is only suggestive analogy rather than a rigorous connection, and |Π| never appears explicitly calibrated or estimated in the experiments, making the practical relevance of the derived rates (which depend on log|Π|) unclear.

Many of the headline theoretical claims (Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.6, Proposition 5.5) are stated as sufficient conditions expressed through complicated, non-transparent functionals (M1-M4, N) defined via nested fixed points and composition of maps (Definition A.2); while mathematically derived, these conditions are difficult to interpret directly and their tightness/necessity is not discussed—only Monte Carlo simulations of the same theoretical constructs are shown to 'match,' which is a weak form of validation since it does not test the assumptions against real generative model behavior, only that the derived formulas behave as the theory predicts on their own terms.

The real-world experimental validation is limited in scope: it uses a single small model (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) and a single synthetic, low-diversity task (shortest path in small graphs, N≤18), with substantial experimental engineering (CP-SAT-based dataset construction to hit precise target Pass@1 and precise β′/Δ curriculum ratios) that makes the setup quite stylized and potentially non-representative of real self-improvement pipelines on natural reasoning tasks (e.g., math, code) where task-difficulty structure is far less controllable and less cleanly power-law-separated.

Some of the correspondence between theory and experiment is only qualitative/directional (e.g., 'first increasing then decreasing' trend in Figure 4a, or the loose claim that the phase-transition budget 'mostly clusters' in 2000-3000), without any quantitative comparison to the actual predicted thresholds (e.g., ν*, νc, νT) from the theory; this leaves open whether the theory's quantitative predictions (not just qualitative shape) are accurate, which limits the strength of the empirical support for such an elaborate theoretical apparatus.

The paper's threat model for 'success' of easy-to-hard is entirely comparative to a fixed-mixture baseline within the same idealized MLE/lower-bound framework; it does not address other realistic complications of practical self-improvement pipelines such as multiple sampled answers combined with more complex verifiers, non-binary/partial rewards, distributional drift beyond difficulty (e.g., style, format), or interaction with RL fine-tuning phases explicitly acknowledged as needed in Remark 4.6.3 but not modeled.

The presentation, while systematic, is extremely dense with many nested definitions, constants, and long appendix derivations (over 60 pages), which may hinder accessibility and independent verification by readers who are not specialists in empirical-process/M-estimation theory; some intuition for why particular functional forms (e.g., power-law difficulty separation, the specific form of Ht/F) are the 'right' modeling choices versus alternatives is not given beyond consistency with the reward-as-difficulty view.

strengths: Addresses a clear gap in prior theory: existing works on self-improvement (sharpening, solver-verifier gap) largely operate in idealized/population or continuous-limit settings, whereas this paper explicitly models the finite-sample regime, which is shown to be essential for explaining why self-improvement neither trivially succeeds nor is model-independent (Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.4).

The 'feedback loop' mechanism (better models accept more data per iteration, which tightens finite-sample bounds) is an intuitive and novel explanation for both sustained improvement and eventual saturation, and is derived rigorously rather than merely asserted.

The extension to easy-to-hard curricula (Section 5) is a genuine and timely theoretical contribution, since most curriculum learning literature is purely empirical; the paper derives explicit feasibility/improvement conditions (Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3, Proposition 5.5) that translate into interpretable practical levers: moderate difficulty separation, critical sample budgets, and phase transitions.

Extensive, careful mathematical development in the appendix (over 40 pages of proofs) with non-trivial techniques (fixed-point/interval analysis via Lemma B.2, asymptotic/Puiseux expansions in Lemma C.2/C.3, monotonicity arguments in Lemma C.8/C.9) suggesting technical solidity.

The theoretical predictions are cross-validated in two complementary ways: Monte Carlo simulations of the abstract bounds (Figures 1-2) and real fine-tuning experiments on a controlled synthetic graph shortest-path task with Llama-3.2-1B (Figures 3-4), and the qualitative trends (moderate difficulty regime, benefit of larger n and m, moderate β' being best, phase transition in required budget) consistently match across both and are also noted to be consistent with prior empirical LLM reasoning literature (Singh et al., Bansal et al., Song et al.).

Clear articulation of contributions and honest discussion of the inherent upper bound on self-improvement (Remark 4.6.3), providing a principled rationale for why practitioners add RL phases after self-improvement.
weaknesses: The framework relies on several strong, somewhat stylized assumptions (Assumption 4.3's coupling constant c and slack γ, Assumption 5.1's power-law difficulty-ratio separation with exponents β, β') whose validity for real LLM reasoning tasks is asserted rather than empirically measured or estimated; it is unclear how one would obtain or verify these constants in practice.

The finite model class Π assumption (needed for the Hellinger-distance MLE argument) is restrictive; the justification in Remark 4.2 (via intrinsic dimensionality and tree-search archives) is suggestive but not rigorous, and |Π| never appears with any concrete estimate in the experiments.

Empirical validation is confined to a single synthetic task (directed graph shortest-path prediction) with a small 1B-parameter model, one candidate per question (m=1 in most curriculum experiments), and relatively small n; there is no test on standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, etc.) that motivate the work throughout the introduction, leaving open how well the theory transfers to the actual verifiable-reward reasoning settings it is designed to explain.

The theory produces only lower bounds on expected reward, and the tightness of these bounds (i.e., how far F°t or the E2H/baseline bounds are from actual observed Pass@1) is not empirically quantified—only qualitative trend-matching is shown, so it's unclear whether the bounds are informative in absolute terms or only in relative/directional terms.

The web of derived quantities (M1-M4, N, β, β', ν, νc, ν*, x±, a0, aL, etc.) is very dense and the practical takeaways depend on interpreting many nested feasibility/improvement conditions; while the remarks help, a reader without working through the appendix may struggle to independently verify or apply the theory, somewhat limiting accessibility and reproducibility of the theoretical claims outside of trusting the paper's own summary.

strengths: Provides a genuinely novel finite-sample, task-centric theoretical framework for iterative self-improvement, going beyond prior population-level/model-evolution analyses (e.g., Huang et al., Sun et al.) by explicitly incorporating sample budgets n and m, model initialization, and task difficulty into concrete lower bounds.

The multi-step self-improvement analysis (Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.4, Proposition 4.5) elegantly explains both sustained improvement and eventual saturation via an iterated-map/fixed-point argument, yielding an interpretable 'feasible initialization interval' whose width depends on sample budget.

The easy-to-hard curriculum analysis (Theorem 5.2, Corollary 5.3, Proposition 5.5, Corollary 5.6) is a substantial technical contribution, deriving explicit feasibility and improvement conditions and characterizing a phase-transition in sample budget and an interior-optimal task-difficulty separation for curriculum benefit — a nontrivial and interesting theoretical prediction.

Extensive, well-designed empirical validation: Monte Carlo simulations directly visualizing the theoretical intervals, a controllable synthetic shortest-path task allowing precise manipulation of initialization/difficulty/budget, and real benchmark experiments (GSM8K, DeepMind Mathematics) across 6 different base models (1B to 32B), showing consistent qualitative agreement with the theory's predictions (moderate difficulty best, larger n/m help, saturation occurs, moderate difficulty ratio optimal for curricula).

The appendix provides complete, careful proofs (including several technical lemmas on cubic root separation, Puiseux expansions, and convexity arguments) that substantiate the claims, which supports reproducibility of the theoretical results.

The paper explicitly ties abstract quantities (β, β′) to the DeepMind Mathematics native difficulty partition via an interpolation parameter ρ, and shows the fitted β, β′ increase with ρ as expected, providing a nice empirical anchor for the abstract exponents.
weaknesses: Several key constants (c, γ in Assumption 4.3; β, β′ in Assumption 5.1) are abstract and not independently measurable in the LLM experiments; they are essentially fit post-hoc from data or treated qualitatively, which weakens the ability to make sharp quantitative (as opposed to qualitative/directional) predictions in practice.

The theoretical guarantees are one-sided lower bounds under a finite model class Π assumption, whose practical relevance for modern LLMs is justified only loosely (via intrinsic-dimension arguments and tree-search-based self-improvement archives), leaving a gap between the idealized theory and actual continuous, high-dimensional parameterizations.

The presentation is very dense, with numerous nested definitions (M1–M4, N, multiple auxiliary intervals I, IM, IN) that, while rigorous, make it difficult for readers to extract clean, actionable takeaways without repeatedly cross-referencing the appendix.

Empirical validation is largely qualitative/trend-level (matching signs and shapes of curves, e.g., 'first increasing then decreasing') rather than quantitative agreement between predicted bound values and observed Pass@1, so the paper does not demonstrate that the derived bounds are tight or numerically predictive.

Some real-benchmark experiments use small per-iteration sample budgets (e.g., n=400–2400) and LoRA fine-tuning with limited epochs, which may not fully represent large-scale production self-improvement pipelines, and the number of random seeds/repetitions for the large-model results (Tables 1–4) is not clearly reported, raising reproducibility/variance concerns.

The easy-to-hard vs. baseline comparison is restricted to two specific schedules (fixed uniform mixture vs. fully staged single-task-per-iteration curriculum via a ρ-interpolation), without exploring other plausible curriculum strategies (e.g., partially overlapping or adaptively scheduled curricula) that practitioners might use.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated open problem: existing self-improvement theory is largely asymptotic/idealized, while this paper provides finite-sample guarantees that explicitly capture the interaction between task difficulty, pretrained initialization, and sample/answer budgets—factors known empirically to matter but previously under-theorized.

The task-centric framing is a genuine conceptual contribution: separating 'when does single-task self-improvement happen' from 'when does easy-to-hard scheduling help' clarifies two distinct empirical phenomena (saturation vs. curriculum benefit) that prior work conflated.

The theory yields concrete, falsifiable, and non-trivial predictions: a moderate-difficulty regime for sustained improvement, an inherent saturation bound below 1, a moderate-difficulty-ratio sweet spot for curricula, and a sample-budget phase transition governing when easy-to-hard beats fixed-mixture training.

Strong and thorough empirical validation: predictions are checked via Monte-Carlo simulation of the theoretical bounds, a fully controllable synthetic shortest-path task, and real benchmarks (GSM8K, DeepMind Mathematics) across six model families/scales (Llama-3.2, Qwen2.5, Qwen3), showing consistent qualitative agreement with theory.

The observed trends (moderate difficulty favored, larger n/m helps, saturation, interior-optimal difficulty ratio for curricula) are also cross-validated against a range of independent prior empirical studies cited in the paper, which strengthens external validity.

The proofs, while dense, are complete and self-contained in the appendix, with careful handling of finite-sample corrections (Hellinger-distance based MLE bounds) and asymptotic expansions (Puiseux series analysis of phase transitions).
weaknesses: The theory rests on several strong stylized assumptions—finite model class Π, the coupling assumption between acceptance rate and reward (Assumption 4.3), and the power-law difficulty-separation assumption (Assumption 5.1)—whose validity for real LLMs is argued only qualitatively (via analogy/citation) rather than empirically verified against the specific models used in experiments.

The key constants (c, γ, cδ, cδ') that govern the bounds are abstract and never estimated from real models; there is no demonstration of how a practitioner would compute these quantities to make the theory actionable, limiting practical applicability despite the paper's predictive claims.

The real-data curriculum experiments (Table 4) show substantial variance (large standard errors relative to effect sizes) and required excluding many DeepMind Mathematics modules (β′ < 0.1 or gap variation < 1%) to obtain a 'measurable' signal, which somewhat weakens the generality/robustness of the empirical support for the improvement condition.

The mapping from theory to real-data estimation of β and β′ (Figure 5) is done post hoc using the initialization model's rewards, but it is unclear how sensitive the qualitative conclusions are to this specific estimation procedure or to measurement noise in β′/β.

The paper's notation and definitional machinery (Mi, N, I(a,ν), multiple nested auxiliary functions) are very dense, which may hinder reproducibility and independent verification by readers outside the immediate proof; a higher-level intuition-first exposition of the key mechanisms would improve accessibility.

Some real-model trajectories contradict the simple 'moderate difficulty is best' narrative in ways not fully explained (e.g., Qwen3-32B's performance decreasing on DeepMind Mathematics despite already-high initial accuracy, and Llama-3.2 models degrading on GSM8K)—while broadly consistent with the theory's saturation/instability predictions, more discussion of these edge cases would strengthen the paper's honesty about the theory's practical boundaries.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap: a finite-sample, task-centric theory of iterative self-improvement that explicitly models the feedback loop between model quality and accepted training data, in contrast to prior asymptotic/population-level treatments (e.g., Huang et al., Sun et al.).

The theoretical development is extensive and internally consistent: single-step and multi-step self-improvement bounds (Thm 4.1, Cor 4.4), the notion of a 'feasible initialization interval' that explains sustained improvement and eventual saturation (Prop 4.5), and an easy-to-hard vs. fixed-mixture comparison with explicit feasibility/improvement conditions (Thm 5.2, Cor 5.3, Prop 5.5) that yield concrete, falsifiable predictions (moderate task difficulty, moderate adjacent-task difficulty ratio, critical sample-budget phase transition).

Strong effort toward empirical validation: a controllable synthetic graph shortest-path task that allows precise manipulation of initialization performance, question/answer budgets, and difficulty ratios, plus real-world validation on GSM8K and DeepMind Mathematics across six model families/sizes (1B–32B parameters), and Monte Carlo simulations that directly visualize the theoretical curves.

The qualitative trends predicted by the theory (moderate-difficulty regime for sustained self-improvement, benefit of larger n and m, saturation with iterations, non-monotonic gain of easy-to-hard curricula as a function of difficulty separation, and budget-dependent phase transition for curriculum benefit) are consistently reproduced across both synthetic and real experiments, lending credibility to the framework.

The paper is transparent about scope and limitations (clean/noiseless reward, connection to but exclusion of test-time training methods) and discusses these candidly in the appendix rather than overselling generality.
weaknesses: The theory rests on several strong, difficult-to-verify structural assumptions: a finite model class Π with bounded log-cardinality (Thm 4.1), the coupling assumption between acceptance rate and expected reward (Assumption 4.3) with unspecified constants c, γ, and the power-law difficulty-separation assumption across tasks (Assumption 5.1) with exponents β, β′ that are only estimated post hoc from data rather than justified a priori.

Validation is largely qualitative/trend-level rather than quantitative: the many nuisance constants in the bounds (cδ, cδ′, c, γ, |Π|) are never estimated or matched to real training runs, so the paper shows that predicted directions of effects hold but does not demonstrate that the actual bounds are numerically informative or tight for real LLMs.

Some reported empirical effects are small relative to their standard errors (e.g., several modules in Table 4, such as div, gcd, place_value have gaps close to zero given their error bars), which somewhat weakens the claimed consistency between theory and the DeepMind Mathematics results.

Experiments use LoRA fine-tuning with a small number of self-improvement iterations (L = 3–4) and often single accepted samples per question (m mostly =1); it is unclear how robust the qualitative conclusions are to full fine-tuning, larger L, or more realistic multi-sample generation/filtering pipelines used in practice.

The paper does not compare its easy-to-hard scheduling predictions against alternative curriculum heuristics used in practice (e.g., adaptive/ability-based scheduling), so it is unclear how the theoretical guidance translates into practical gains beyond the specific ρ-interpolation baseline constructed for the experiments.

The manuscript is extremely dense (69 pages including a lengthy, highly technical appendix), and the sheer number of interacting constants, auxiliary maps (F, Ht, G, Mi, N ) and asymptotic regimes makes independent verification and practical uptake by readers challenging.
